claim: Adult-born granule cells (abGCs) project to the CA2 region of the hippocampus.
source: Adult-born granule cells (abGCs) project to the CA2 region of the hippocampus, but it remains unknown how this circuit affects behavioral function.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as background information and verified with immunohistochemistry using 3R-Tau marker in Figure 1a.

claim: Ablation of abGCs impaired the ability to discriminate between a caregiving mother and a novel mother.
source: Ablation of abGCs impaired the ability to discriminate between a caregiving mother and a novel mother, and this ability returned after abGCs were regenerated.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally using GFAP-TK mice with VGCV administration, shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The ability to discriminate between caregiving mother and novel mother returned after abGCs were regenerated.
source: Ablation of abGCs impaired the ability to discriminate between a caregiving mother and a novel mother, and this ability returned after abGCs were regenerated.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally after cessation of VGCV treatment, shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of projections from abGCs to the CA2 temporarily prevented the retrieval of remote mother memories.
source: Chemogenetic inhibition of projections from abGCs to the CA2 also temporarily prevented the retrieval of remote mother memories.
evidence: Demonstrated using Nestin-cre:Gi mice with CNO infusion, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The effect of abGC inhibition on mother memory retrieval was observed when abGCs were inhibited at 4–6 weeks old.
source: These findings were observed when abGCs were inhibited at 4–6 weeks old, but not when they were inhibited at 10–12 weeks old.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally with age-specific cohorts of abGCs, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The effect of abGC inhibition on mother memory retrieval was not observed when abGCs were inhibited at 10–12 weeks old.
source: These findings were observed when abGCs were inhibited at 4–6 weeks old, but not when they were inhibited at 10–12 weeks old.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally with age-specific cohorts of abGCs, shown in Figure 2f.

claim: abGCs are necessary for differentiating features of CA2 network activity, including theta-gamma coupling and sharp wave ripples, in response to novel versus familiar social stimuli.
source: We also found that abGCs are necessary for differentiating features of CA2 network activity, including theta-gamma coupling and sharp wave ripples, in response to novel versus familiar social stimuli.
evidence: Demonstrated through electrophysiological recordings in CA2, shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: abGCs are necessary for neuronal oscillations associated with discriminating between social stimuli.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that abGCs are necessary for neuronal oscillations associated with discriminating between social stimuli, thus enabling retrieval of remote developmental memories of the mother by their adult offspring.
evidence: Inferred from combined behavioral and electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mice can recognize their mothers and distinguish them from unfamiliar mothers during the first postnatal week.
source: Mice can also recognize their mothers and distinguish them from unfamiliar mothers during the first postnatal week (Laham et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Laham et al., 2021.

claim: Memories of the mother last well into adulthood in mice.
source: These memories last well into adulthood, with a reversal in social preference at the time of weaning (Laham et al., 2021); pup offspring prefer investigating their own mothers over novel mothers, while adult offspring prefer investigating unfamiliar mothers over their own.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Laham et al., 2021.

claim: There is a reversal in social preference at the time of weaning, with pup offspring preferring their own mothers and adult offspring preferring unfamiliar mothers.
source: These memories last well into adulthood, with a reversal in social preference at the time of weaning (Laham et al., 2021); pup offspring prefer investigating their own mothers over novel mothers, while adult offspring prefer investigating unfamiliar mothers over their own.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Laham et al., 2021.

claim: In adulthood, the ability to discriminate between the caregiving mother and a novel mother persists despite no contact with the mother for over a month after weaning.
source: In adulthood, the ability to discriminate between the caregiving mother and a novel mother persists despite any contact with the mother for over a month after weaning.
evidence: Stated as background information based on previous findings.

claim: Lower investigation times of the mother compared to a novel mother suggest retrieval of a remote social memory by adult offspring.
source: Lower investigation times of the mother compared to a novel mother suggest retrieval of a remote social memory by adult offspring.
evidence: Interpretation of behavioral data based on established principles of social recognition.

claim: The CA2 region of the hippocampus is required for the ability to recognize caregiving mothers and distinguish them from novel mothers both during development and in adulthood.
source: The CA2 region of the hippocampus is required for the ability to recognize caregiving mothers and distinguish them from novel mothers both during development and in adulthood (Laham et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Laham et al., 2021.

claim: The CA2 is necessary for short-term memory of peers during development and in adulthood.
source: The CA2 is also necessary for short-term memory of peers during development and in adulthood (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Smith et al., 2016; Laham et al., 2021; Diethorn and Gould, 2023).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Rhythmic firing in the CA2 supports the social memory functions of this region.
source: A growing literature suggests that rhythmic firing in the CA2 supports the social memory functions of this region.
evidence: Stated as a summary of existing literature.

claim: Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) of low frequency theta rhythm with higher frequency gamma rhythm in the CA2 is increased by exposure to familiar peers.
source: Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) of low frequency theta rhythm with higher frequency gamma rhythm in the CA2 and the generation of sharp wave ripples (SWRs), high frequency bursts in the CA2, are increased by exposure to familiar peers and short-term consolidation of social memory for peers, respectively (Zhu et al., 2023; Oliva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2023 and Oliva et al., 2020.

claim: The generation of sharp wave ripples (SWRs) in the CA2 is increased by short-term consolidation of social memory for peers.
source: Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) of low frequency theta rhythm with higher frequency gamma rhythm in the CA2 and the generation of sharp wave ripples (SWRs), high frequency bursts in the CA2, are increased by exposure to familiar peers and short-term consolidation of social memory for peers, respectively (Zhu et al., 2023; Oliva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2023 and Oliva et al., 2020.

claim: In CA1 and CA3, PAC and SWRs have been associated with novelty detection, memory consolidation, and memory retrieval of nonsocial stimuli and events over relatively short time frames.
source: In other hippocampal subregions, namely the CA1 and CA3, PAC and SWRs have been associated with novelty detection, memory consolidation, and memory retrieval of nonsocial stimuli and events over relatively short time frames (Colgin, 2015; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Joo and Frank, 2018; Meier et al., 2020; Vivekananda et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Certain patterns of oscillatory firing may facilitate replay and pre-play of neuronal ensembles activated during specific experiences.
source: These studies suggest that certain patterns of oscillatory firing may facilitate replay and pre-play of neuronal ensembles activated during specific experiences (Joo and Frank, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Joo and Frank, 2018.

claim: No previous studies have examined whether PAC and SWRs are associated with retrieval of remote developmental memories.
source: However, no previous studies have examined whether PAC and SWRs are associated with retrieval of remote developmental memories.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current study based on literature review.

claim: The CA2 has been called a social memory 'hub' because it receives and integrates inputs from multiple brain areas.
source: The CA2 has been called a social memory 'hub' because it receives and integrates inputs from multiple brain areas (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Oliva et al., 2020; Diethorn and Gould, 2023), including from granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Kohara et al., 2014), a population known to undergo adult neurogenesis (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The CA2 receives inputs from granule cells of the dentate gyrus.
source: The CA2 has been called a social memory 'hub' because it receives and integrates inputs from multiple brain areas (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Oliva et al., 2020; Diethorn and Gould, 2023), including from granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Kohara et al., 2014), a population known to undergo adult neurogenesis (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohara et al., 2014.

claim: Granule cells of the dentate gyrus undergo adult neurogenesis.
source: The CA2 has been called a social memory 'hub' because it receives and integrates inputs from multiple brain areas (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Oliva et al., 2020; Diethorn and Gould, 2023), including from granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Kohara et al., 2014), a population known to undergo adult neurogenesis (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2012.

claim: abGCs are important for discriminating between novel and familiar peers.
source: abGCs are important for discriminating between novel and familiar peers (Pereira-Caixeta et al., 2018; Cope et al., 2020), and although these cells are known to project to the CA2 (Llorens-Martín et al., 2015), the function of this circuit remains unexplored.
evidence: Supported by citations to Pereira-Caixeta et al., 2018 and Cope et al., 2020.

claim: abGCs project to the CA2.
source: abGCs are important for discriminating between novel and familiar peers (Pereira-Caixeta et al., 2018; Cope et al., 2020), and although these cells are known to project to the CA2 (Llorens-Martín et al., 2015), the function of this circuit remains unexplored.
evidence: Supported by citation to Llorens-Martín et al., 2015.

claim: The function of the abGC-CA2 circuit remains unexplored.
source: abGCs are important for discriminating between novel and familiar peers (Pereira-Caixeta et al., 2018; Cope et al., 2020), and although these cells are known to project to the CA2 (Llorens-Martín et al., 2015), the function of this circuit remains unexplored.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current study based on literature review.

claim: The dentate gyrus influences hippocampal gamma oscillations, PAC, and SWRs in general.
source: Furthermore, although the dentate gyrus is known to influence hippocampal gamma oscillations, PAC, and SWRs in general (Bott et al., 2016; Meier et al., 2020; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021), no studies have examined the influence of abGCs on these oscillatory patterns in the CA2 specifically.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bott et al., 2016; Meier et al., 2020; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021.

claim: No studies have examined the influence of abGCs on oscillatory patterns in the CA2 specifically.
source: Furthermore, although the dentate gyrus is known to influence hippocampal gamma oscillations, PAC, and SWRs in general (Bott et al., 2016; Meier et al., 2020; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2021), no studies have examined the influence of abGCs on these oscillatory patterns in the CA2 specifically.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current study based on literature review.

claim: 3R-Tau is a marker of abGC axons.
source: In the CA2, we verified abGC projections using 3R-Tau, a marker of abGC axons (Llorens-Martín et al., 2015), as well as mature granule cell projections using ZnT3, a marker of mature mossy fibers (Wenzel et al., 1997; Figure 1a and ai–aiii).
evidence: Supported by citation to Llorens-Martín et al., 2015.

claim: ZnT3 is a marker of mature mossy fibers.
source: In the CA2, we verified abGC projections using 3R-Tau, a marker of abGC axons (Llorens-Martín et al., 2015), as well as mature granule cell projections using ZnT3, a marker of mature mossy fibers (Wenzel et al., 1997; Figure 1a and ai–aiii).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wenzel et al., 1997.

claim: abGC projections to the CA2 are preferentially associated with the proximal dendrites of parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons compared to the proximal dendrites of pyramidal cells.
source: We further determined that abGC projections to the CA2 are preferentially associated with the proximal dendrites of parvalbumin-positive (PV +) interneurons labeled with cre-dependent AAV mCherry compared to the proximal dendrites of pyramidal cells immunolabeled with PCP4 (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: Demonstrated through immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 1b-d.

claim: The preferential association of abGC projections with PV+ interneurons over pyramidal cells mirrors abGC projection patterns to the CA3.
source: Although we cannot determine whether a similar relationship exists with projections to distal dendrites or whether these connections represent active synapses, this preferential association with PV + interneurons over pyramidal cells mirrors abGC projection patterns to the CA3 (Restivo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Restivo et al., 2015.

claim: The CA2 region is involved in the retrieval of remote developmental memories.
source: Because the CA2 region is involved in the retrieval of remote developmental memories (Laham et al., 2021) and abGCs have been linked to the storage and retrieval of recently encountered mice (Cope et al., 2020), we next investigated whether abGCs are necessary for the retrieval of developmental memories of the mother.
evidence: Supported by citation to Laham et al., 2021.

claim: abGCs have been linked to the storage and retrieval of recently encountered mice.
source: Because the CA2 region is involved in the retrieval of remote developmental memories (Laham et al., 2021) and abGCs have been linked to the storage and retrieval of recently encountered mice (Cope et al., 2020), we next investigated whether abGCs are necessary for the retrieval of developmental memories of the mother.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cope et al., 2020.

claim: Adult GFAP-TK mice and CD1 littermates with control levels of abGCs investigate their own mother less than a novel mother.
source: Using the GFAP-TK transgenic mouse model in which abGCs are ablated upon valganciclovir (VGCV) administration (Snyder et al., 2011), we found that adult GFAP-TK mice and CD1 littermates with control levels of abGCs investigate their own mother less than a novel mother (Figure 1e–g, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a), similar to what has been observed in C57 mice (Laham et al., 2021).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1e-g.

claim: Adult mice prefer novel stimuli over familiar stimuli.
source: Because adult mice prefer novel stimuli over familiar stimuli, lower investigation times of previously encountered mice compared to novel mice can be interpreted as recognition.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mouse behavior.

claim: Lower investigation times of previously encountered mice compared to novel mice can be interpreted as recognition.
source: Because adult mice prefer novel stimuli over familiar stimuli, lower investigation times of previously encountered mice compared to novel mice can be interpreted as recognition.
evidence: Interpretation based on established behavioral principles.

claim: Adult mice with intact abGCs can recognize mothers as familiar even after being separated since weaning.
source: Thus, our social investigation data in adult mice with intact abGCs suggest that these mice can recognize mothers as familiar even after being separated since weaning (at P21).
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data showing differential investigation times.

claim: Mice with depleted abGCs are no longer able to discriminate between their own mother and a novel mother.
source: In contrast, mice with depleted abGCs are no longer able to discriminate between their own mother and a novel mother, as indicated by investigation times (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: No changes were observed in overall locomotion during social trials after abGC depletion.
source: No changes were observed in overall locomotion during social trials after abGC depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), suggesting that any physical activity differences between groups are not responsible for differences in social investigation times.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Cessation of VGCV treatment in GFAP-TK mice enabled a 70% recovery of abGCs in the DG.
source: Cessation of VGCV treatment in GFAP-TK mice enabled a 70% recovery of abGCs in the DG (Figure 1h, j and k) and complete recovery of abGC 3R-Tau+ axon intensity in the CA2 (Figure 1i, l and m).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1h, j, k.

claim: Cessation of VGCV treatment in GFAP-TK mice enabled complete recovery of abGC 3R-Tau+ axon intensity in the CA2.
source: Cessation of VGCV treatment in GFAP-TK mice enabled a 70% recovery of abGCs in the DG (Figure 1h, j and k) and complete recovery of abGC 3R-Tau+ axon intensity in the CA2 (Figure 1i, l and m).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1i, l, m.

claim: Coinciding with the recovery of adult neurogenesis, GFAP-TK animals regained the ability to discriminate between their mother and a novel mother with differential investigation times.
source: Coinciding with the recovery of adult neurogenesis, GFAP-TK animals regained the ability to discriminate between their mother and a novel mother with differential investigation times (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: abGCs are not necessary for maintaining developmental social memories, but instead support retrieval of remote memories of the mother.
source: These results reveal that abGCs are not necessary for maintaining developmental social memories, but instead support retrieval of remote memories of the mother.
evidence: Inferred from the ablation and recovery experiments showing that memory persists during abGC depletion but cannot be retrieved.

claim: abGCs are important for nonsocial memories only during a limited time after they are generated, i.e., 4–6 weeks after mitosis.
source: Previous studies have shown that abGCs are important for nonsocial memories only during a limited time after they are generated, i.e., 4–6 weeks after mitosis (Gu et al., 2012; Song et al., 2012; Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gu et al., 2012; Song et al., 2012; Kropff et al., 2015.

claim: Nestin-cre:Gi mice investigated the mother less than the novel mother when vehicle was infused.
source: As expected, we found that Nestin-cre:Gi mice investigated the mother less than the novel mother when vehicle was infused; however, inhibition of this pathway after CNO infusion in CA2 prevented this ability (Figure 2e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Inhibition of the abGC-CA2 pathway after CNO infusion prevented the ability to discriminate between mother and novel mother.
source: As expected, we found that Nestin-cre:Gi mice investigated the mother less than the novel mother when vehicle was infused; however, inhibition of this pathway after CNO infusion in CA2 prevented this ability (Figure 2e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: There were no differences in locomotion at baseline or during the social trials in any groups.
source: There were no differences in locomotion at baseline or during the social trials in any groups, suggesting that the effects of social investigation time were not the result of physical activity differences (Figure 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: CNO treatment in the same abGC cohort 6 weeks later (10–12 week-old abGCs) had no effect on Nestin-cre:Gi animals' ability to discriminate between their mother and a novel mother.
source: CNO treatment in the same abGC cohort 6 weeks later (10–12 week-old abGCs) had no effect on Nestin-cre:Gi animals' ability to discriminate between their mother and a novel mother (Figure 2f, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 2f.

claim: abGCs are required for retrieving remote social memories of the mother when the cells are immature (4–6 weeks post-mitosis), but not when they are mature (10–12 weeks post-mitosis).
source: These findings suggest that abGCs are required for retrieving remote social memories of the mother when the cells are immature (4–6 weeks post-mitosis), but not when they are mature (10–12 weeks post-mitosis), presumably because a younger abGC cohort has taken over this function.
evidence: Inferred from the age-specific effects of abGC inhibition on behavior.

claim: A younger abGC cohort has taken over the function of retrieving remote social memories when older abGCs mature.
source: These findings suggest that abGCs are required for retrieving remote social memories of the mother when the cells are immature (4–6 weeks post-mitosis), but not when they are mature (10–12 weeks post-mitosis), presumably because a younger abGC cohort has taken over this function.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the age-specific effects observed.

claim: CNO may have affected abGC terminals in the nearby CA3a region in addition to CA2.
source: It should be noted that although cannula were placed over the CA2 region, we cannot rule out the possibility that CNO affected abGC terminals in the nearby CA3a region.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Immature abGCs were silenced immediately after the investigation of a novel adult mouse in a social memory consolidation experiment.
source: An additional experiment explored if abGCs contribute to peer social memory consolidation (Figure 2g). Immature abGCs were silenced immediately after the investigation of a novel adult mouse.
evidence: Described as part of the experimental design shown in Figure 2g.

claim: When reintroduced to the now familiar adult mouse 6 hr later, mice exhibited control-like social discrimination.
source: When reintroduced to the now familiar adult mouse 6 hr later, a time at which studies have shown that the effects of CNO on other behaviors have worn off (Alexander et al., 2009; Whissell et al., 2016; Ray et al., 2011), mice exhibited control-like social discrimination (Figure 2h), suggesting that abGC activity may not be required for social memory consolidation.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The effects of CNO on other behaviors have worn off by 6 hr after treatment.
source: When reintroduced to the now familiar adult mouse 6 hr later, a time at which studies have shown that the effects of CNO on other behaviors have worn off (Alexander et al., 2009; Whissell et al., 2016; Ray et al., 2011), mice exhibited control-like social discrimination (Figure 2h), suggesting that abGC activity may not be required for social memory consolidation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Alexander et al., 2009; Whissell et al., 2016; Ray et al., 2011.

claim: abGC activity may not be required for social memory consolidation.
source: When reintroduced to the now familiar adult mouse 6 hr later, a time at which studies have shown that the effects of CNO on other behaviors have worn off (Alexander et al., 2009; Whissell et al., 2016; Ray et al., 2011), mice exhibited control-like social discrimination (Figure 2h), suggesting that abGC activity may not be required for social memory consolidation.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results shown in Figure 2h.

claim: SWR production is increased during exposure to a social stimulus.
source: We found that SWR production (Figure 3c and d) is increased during exposure to a social stimulus (Figure 3e and k), and that more SWRs are produced during novel mother exposure, presumably during encoding social memories, than during mother exposure, presumably during retrieval of developmental social memories (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3e and k.

claim: More SWRs are produced during novel mother exposure than during mother exposure.
source: We found that SWR production (Figure 3c and d) is increased during exposure to a social stimulus (Figure 3e and k), and that more SWRs are produced during novel mother exposure, presumably during encoding social memories, than during mother exposure, presumably during retrieval of developmental social memories (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Novel mother exposure is associated with encoding social memories.
source: We found that SWR production (Figure 3c and d) is increased during exposure to a social stimulus (Figure 3e and k), and that more SWRs are produced during novel mother exposure, presumably during encoding social memories, than during mother exposure, presumably during retrieval of developmental social memories (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Inferred interpretation of the behavioral context.

claim: Mother exposure is associated with retrieval of developmental social memories.
source: We found that SWR production (Figure 3c and d) is increased during exposure to a social stimulus (Figure 3e and k), and that more SWRs are produced during novel mother exposure, presumably during encoding social memories, than during mother exposure, presumably during retrieval of developmental social memories (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Inferred interpretation of the behavioral context.

claim: Inhibition of abGCs in the presence of a social stimulus altered several features of SWR production, including decreasing SWR frequency, integral, and duration.
source: However, inhibition of abGCs in the presence of a social stimulus altered several features of SWR production, including decreasing SWR frequency, integral, and duration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), but no effects on SWR peak amplitude (Figure 3h).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Inhibition of abGCs had no effects on SWR peak amplitude during social stimulus exposure.
source: However, inhibition of abGCs in the presence of a social stimulus altered several features of SWR production, including decreasing SWR frequency, integral, and duration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a), but no effects on SWR peak amplitude (Figure 3h).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Inhibition of abGCs during baseline recordings showed no change in SWR frequency.
source: Inhibition of abGCs during baseline recordings showed no change in SWR frequency, but an increase in SWR peak amplitude (Figure 3i and j).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Inhibition of abGCs during baseline recordings showed an increase in SWR peak amplitude.
source: Inhibition of abGCs during baseline recordings showed no change in SWR frequency, but an increase in SWR peak amplitude (Figure 3i and j).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Inhibition of 10–12 week-old abGCs had no statistically significant effect on social novelty-induced increases in CA2 SWRs.
source: Conversely, inhibition of 10–12 week-old abGCs had no statistically significant effect on social novelty-induced increases in CA2 SWRs, nor did it affect other features of SWR production (Figure 3k, Figure 3—figure supplements 1d, e and 2b).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3k, Figure 3—figure supplements 1d, e and 2b.

claim: Inhibition of 10–12 week-old abGCs did not affect other features of SWR production.
source: Conversely, inhibition of 10–12 week-old abGCs had no statistically significant effect on social novelty-induced increases in CA2 SWRs, nor did it affect other features of SWR production (Figure 3k, Figure 3—figure supplements 1d, e and 2b).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3k, Figure 3—figure supplements 1d, e and 2b.

claim: 4–6-week-old abGCs, but not 10–12-week-old abGCs, are necessary for promoting appropriate SWR responses during social novelty exploration and developmental social memory retrieval.
source: These findings suggest that 4–6-week-old abGCs, but not 10–12-week-old abGCs, are necessary for promoting appropriate SWR responses during social novelty exploration and developmental social memory retrieval.
evidence: Inferred from the age-specific effects of abGC inhibition on SWRs.

claim: CA2 SWR generation was suppressed upon exposure to a nonsocial stimulus.
source: In an additional study, we investigated if CA2 SWRs were modulated by the presence of a nonsocial stimulus (an object) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–f). Surprisingly, CA2 SWR generation was suppressed upon exposure to a nonsocial stimulus (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Inhibiting immature abGCs had no statistically significant effects on SWR features in response to a nonsocial stimulus.
source: Inhibiting immature abGCs had no statistically significant effects on SWR features in response to a nonsocial stimulus (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b–e).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b–e.

claim: Exposure to the mother was associated with increased theta-mid-gamma PAC.
source: We found that exposure to the mother was associated with increased theta-mid-gamma PAC, and that this increase was prevented after inhibition of 4–6-week-old abGCs (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4b–d.

claim: The increase in theta-mid-gamma PAC during mother exposure was prevented after inhibition of 4–6-week-old abGCs.
source: We found that exposure to the mother was associated with increased theta-mid-gamma PAC, and that this increase was prevented after inhibition of 4–6-week-old abGCs (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4b–d.

claim: 4–6-week-old abGCs had no influence on CA2 oscillation power across theta, low-gamma, and mid-gamma frequency bands.
source: Conversely, 4–6-week-old abGCs had no influence on CA2 oscillation power across theta, low-gamma, and mid-gamma frequency bands (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–f).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–f.

claim: Inhibition of a 10–12-week-old cohort of abGCs had no statistically significant effect on PAC signatures evoked during exposure to the mother.
source: Inhibition of a 10–12-week-old cohort of abGCs had no statistically significant effect on PAC signatures evoked during exposure to the mother (Figure 4e–g), although there appears to be an overall shift in gamma phase within theta cycles, especially during the mother exposure condition (Figure 4g).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4e–g.

claim: There appears to be an overall shift in gamma phase within theta cycles after inhibition of 10–12-week-old abGCs, especially during the mother exposure condition.
source: Inhibition of a 10–12-week-old cohort of abGCs had no statistically significant effect on PAC signatures evoked during exposure to the mother (Figure 4e–g), although there appears to be an overall shift in gamma phase within theta cycles, especially during the mother exposure condition (Figure 4g).
evidence: Observed in the data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: abGC influence on CA2 network activity is limited to a specific abGC age range.
source: This suggests that abGC influence on CA2 network activity is limited to a specific abGC age range.
evidence: Inferred from the age-specific effects observed in the PAC experiments.

claim: 4–6-week-old abGCs support CA2 network oscillations present during both encoding and retrieval of social memories.
source: Taken together with our SWR results, these findings suggest that 4–6-week-old abGCs support CA2 network oscillations present during both encoding and retrieval of social memories.
evidence: Inferred from the combined SWR and PAC results.

claim: Hippocampal CA2 plays an important role in supporting social recognition.
source: Hippocampal CA2 plays an important role in supporting social recognition (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Smith et al., 2016; Laham et al., 2021; Diethorn and Gould, 2023), yet the contributions of the abGC projection to this region have remained uninvestigated.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The contributions of the abGC projection to CA2 have remained uninvestigated.
source: Hippocampal CA2 plays an important role in supporting social recognition (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Smith et al., 2016; Laham et al., 2021; Diethorn and Gould, 2023), yet the contributions of the abGC projection to this region have remained uninvestigated.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Recovery of abGCs and their projections to CA2 restored the ability to discriminate between novel mothers and caregiving mothers.
source: Recovery of abGCs and their projections to CA2 restored the ability to discriminate between novel mothers and caregiving mothers, revealing that abGCs support developmental social memory retrieval and not remote memory storage.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the ablation and recovery experiments.

claim: abGCs support developmental social memory retrieval and not remote memory storage.
source: Recovery of abGCs and their projections to CA2 restored the ability to discriminate between novel mothers and caregiving mothers, revealing that abGCs support developmental social memory retrieval and not remote memory storage.
evidence: Inferred from the ablation and recovery experiments showing that memory persists during abGC depletion.

claim: abGCs possess a time-sensitive ability to support retrieval of developmental mother memories.
source: This effect was not detected when inhibiting 10–12-week-old abGC projections, revealing that abGCs possess a time-sensitive ability to support retrieval of developmental mother memories.
evidence: Inferred from the age-specific effects of abGC inhibition.

claim: Projections from abGCs to the CA3 may have been affected in double transgenic mice with CNO infusion.
source: It is important to note that we cannot rule out the possibility that projections from abGCs to the CA3 were also affected in double transgenic mice with CNO infusion, due to the potential diffusion of the drug away from the CA2 cannula site.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: The ventral CA3 is involved in social recognition.
source: Along these lines, studies have shown that the ventral CA3 is also involved in social recognition (Chiang et al., 2018) and that areas CA2 and CA3 may act together to coordinate replay (Stöber et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chiang et al., 2018 and Stöber et al., 2020.

claim: Areas CA2 and CA3 may act together to coordinate replay.
source: Along these lines, studies have shown that the ventral CA3 is also involved in social recognition (Chiang et al., 2018) and that areas CA2 and CA3 may act together to coordinate replay (Stöber et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stöber et al., 2020.

claim: The abGC-CA2 circuit may work in concert with the abGC-CA3 circuit, followed by crosstalk between the two target areas to mediate social recognition.
source: Thus, the abGC-CA2 circuit may work in concert with the abGC-CA3 circuit, followed by crosstalk between the two target areas to mediate social recognition.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the potential involvement of both CA2 and CA3.

claim: Exposure to novel mothers produced a larger increase in CA2 SWR frequency than exposure to caregiving mothers.
source: We also investigated if abGCs support developmental mother memory retrieval via modulation of CA2 network activity and found that exposure to novel mothers produced a larger increase in CA2 SWR frequency than exposure to caregiving mothers.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the electrophysiology recordings.

claim: CA2 theta/mid-gamma PAC was higher during exposure to caregiving mothers than to novel mothers.
source: We also found the converse with CA2 theta/mid-gamma PAC, which was higher during exposure to caregiving mothers than to novel mothers.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Both SWR and PAC effects were significantly diminished after inhibiting 4–6-week-old abGCs.
source: Both effects were significantly diminished after inhibiting 4–6-week-old abGCs.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in the electrophysiology recordings.

claim: Inhibition of immature abGCs alters SWR generation and theta-mid-gamma PAC in the CA2 region in a way that increases network activity similarity across novel and familiar social interactions.
source: Thus, inhibition of immature abGCs alters SWR generation and theta-mid-gamma PAC in the CA2 region in a way that increases network activity similarity across novel and familiar social interactions.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing reduced differentiation between conditions.

claim: Inhibiting CA2 activity alters both SWRs and gamma oscillations in CA1.
source: These changes likely affect broader hippocampal circuitry as inhibiting CA2 activity alters both SWRs and gamma oscillations in CA1 (Alexander et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alexander et al., 2018 and Brown et al., 2020.

claim: abGC inhibition of network orthogonalization may contribute to the inability to socially discriminate.
source: abGC inhibition of network orthogonalization may contribute to the inability to socially discriminate.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying behavioral effects.

claim: abGCs contribute to the diversification of neuronal oscillatory states in the CA2 in the service of both recognizing social novelty and retrieving developmental social memories.
source: Our data suggest that abGCs contribute to the diversification of neuronal oscillatory states in the CA2 in the service of both recognizing social novelty and retrieving developmental social memories.
evidence: Inferred from the combined behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claim: CA2 SWRs correspond with the activation of neuronal ensembles that are associated with previous social experience, at least during sleep.
source: Although we did not record single units along with neuronal oscillations, previous studies suggest that CA2 SWRs correspond with the activation of neuronal ensembles that are associated with previous social experience, at least during sleep (Oliva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oliva et al., 2020.

claim: By promoting the generation of SWRs during social, especially novel, experience, abGCs may provide a network conducive to replay.
source: Thus, by promoting the generation of SWRs during social, especially novel, experience, abGCs may provide a network conducive to replay.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the role of SWRs in replay.

claim: The ability of abGCs to facilitate the generation of SWRs and PAC may be related to their preferential connections to PV+ interneurons.
source: The ability of abGCs to facilitate the generation of SWRs and PAC may be related to their preferential connections to PV + interneurons, which have been causally linked to SWRs, as well as to theta and gamma oscillations (Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Amilhon et al., 2015; Gan et al., 2017; Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020; Kriener et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by multiple citations to previous work on PV+ interneurons.

claim: PV+ interneurons have been causally linked to SWRs, as well as to theta and gamma oscillations.
source: The ability of abGCs to facilitate the generation of SWRs and PAC may be related to their preferential connections to PV + interneurons, which have been causally linked to SWRs, as well as to theta and gamma oscillations (Schlingloff et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2014; Amilhon et al., 2015; Gan et al., 2017; Antonoudiou et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020; Kriener et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: A time-limited role for abGCs in nonsocial memory has been previously reported.
source: A time-limited role for abGCs in nonsocial memory has been previously reported (Gu et al., 2012; Song et al., 2012; Swan et al., 2014; Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: abGCs are highly excitable and exhibit enhanced synaptic plasticity 4–6 weeks after their generation.
source: Previous studies have shown that abGCs are highly excitable and exhibit enhanced synaptic plasticity 4–6 weeks after their generation, and that these properties appear to be diminished by 8 weeks post-mitosis (Song et al., 2012; Toni and Schinder, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Song et al., 2012 and Toni and Schinder, 2015.

claim: The enhanced excitability and synaptic plasticity properties of abGCs appear to be diminished by 8 weeks post-mitosis.
source: Previous studies have shown that abGCs are highly excitable and exhibit enhanced synaptic plasticity 4–6 weeks after their generation, and that these properties appear to be diminished by 8 weeks post-mitosis (Song et al., 2012; Toni and Schinder, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Song et al., 2012 and Toni and Schinder, 2015.

claim: As abGCs mature and become more inhibited, they may function to provide input to the CA2 only when social stimuli are especially salient, such as when they are threatening or associated with a potent reward.
source: As abGCs mature and become more inhibited, they may function to provide input to the CA2 only when social stimuli are especially salient, such as when they are threatening or associated with a potent reward.
evidence: Speculative interpretation about the function of mature abGCs.

claim: It may be relevant to determine whether abGC inputs to the CA2 affect synaptic input from the supramammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus.
source: It may also be relevant to determine whether abGC inputs to the CA2 affect synaptic input from the supramammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus, which is known to respond to social novelty (Chen et al., 2020) and drive novelty-induced increases in adult neurogenesis (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative suggestion for future research supported by citations to Chen et al., 2020 and Li et al., 2022.

claim: The supramammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus is known to respond to social novelty.
source: It may also be relevant to determine whether abGC inputs to the CA2 affect synaptic input from the supramammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus, which is known to respond to social novelty (Chen et al., 2020) and drive novelty-induced increases in adult neurogenesis (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: The supramammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus drives novelty-induced increases in adult neurogenesis.
source: It may also be relevant to determine whether abGC inputs to the CA2 affect synaptic input from the supramammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus, which is known to respond to social novelty (Chen et al., 2020) and drive novelty-induced increases in adult neurogenesis (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: abGCs may influence the supramammillary-CA2 circuit by increasing excitatory tone in the same target cells, which in turn alters neuronal oscillations.
source: It is possible that abGCs influence this circuit by increasing excitatory tone in the same target cells, which in turn alters neuronal oscillations, although this hypothesis remains untested.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about mechanism.

claim: VGCV administration produces a dramatic loss of abGCs (3R-Tau+ cells) in DG.
source: VGCV administration produces a dramatic loss of (h-hii) abGCs (3R-Tau + cells) in DG (VGCV-: n=8; VGCV+: n=8; unpaired t-test: t14=6.588, p<0.0001)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1h-hii with statistical analysis.

claim: 6 weeks after removing VGCV from the rodent chow, DG abGC number undergoes a 70% recovery.
source: 6 weeks after removing VGCV from the rodent chow, DG abGC number (j, k) undergoes a 70% recovery (CD1: n=8; TK: n=8; unpaired t-test: t14=3.218, p=0.0062)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1j, k with statistical analysis.

claim: abGC fibers (3R-Tau+) in the CA2 are more abundant near proximal dendrites of PV+ interneurons than those of pyramidal cells.
source: (d) abGC fibers (3R-Tau+) in the CA2 are more abundant near proximal dendrites (n=7; paired t-test: t6=3.163, p=0.0195) of PV + interneurons (mCherry+) than those of pyramidal cells (PCP4+).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1d with statistical analysis.
